llm.summary: This skill is mostly coherent, but it can change or permanently delete live blog content and its token handling can expose credentials if misconfigured.

dimensions.detail: The CLI reads a bearer token from a config file, environment variable, or command-line argument and sends it to the configured blog domain without enforcing HTTPS or validating the destination host.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The package contains a manifest, SKILL.md, and a local Python CLI; no install-time remote code fetch, tool spoofing, scheduled task, or hidden installer behavior was found.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill includes broad activation keywords for blog, archive, and knowledge-base tasks, while the runtime CLI can immediately perform write and delete operations; the skill text requires delete confirmation, but the CLI itself has no confirmation or dry-run interlock.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The skill documents persistent plaintext token storage under ~/.config/typecho-cli/config.json and supports --token arguments, but does not document restrictive file permissions or warn against shell-history/log exposure; no background persistence was found.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The artifacts consistently describe a Typecho blog-management skill that lists, reads, creates, updates, and deletes posts through typecho-cli; those capabilities fit the stated purpose but affect live public content.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Review before installing on a production blog. Use only an HTTPS Typecho URL you control, avoid passing the token with --token, store the config file with restrictive permissions, and require explicit confirmation before any update or delete action. Rotate the Typecho token if it may have been sent over HTTP, stored in logs, or shared with another agent.
llm.findings:
[LP3] expected: Filesystem config access, environment-variable access, and network calls are expected for a self-hosted blog CLI, but the artifact would benefit from explicit permission boundaries around the config path, token variables, and Typecho endpoint.
[SQP-1] unexpected: The broad trigger wording is not necessary for direct blog publishing and could activate the skill for ambiguous archive or knowledge-base requests despite its live mutation authority.
[SQP-3] expected: Chinese-only documentation and CLI help match the artifact language and are not a security concern by themselves, though users should understand the prompts before allowing blog changes.
[SQP-2] expected: Managing and deleting posts is purpose-aligned and disclosed, but the irreversible delete path needs stronger runtime safeguards because the CLI executes deletion immediately when invoked.
[T09] unexpected: Accepting arbitrary configured domains without requiring HTTPS is not required for safe Typecho publishing and can expose the bearer token and blog content over an unencrypted or attacker-controlled endpoint.
[T09] unexpected: Plaintext token storage and command-line token support are common CLI patterns but are under-documented here because there is no permission check or warning about shell history and logs.
